before.title: Engine ECU/ECM electrolytic capacitor leakage (age-related)
before.description: The surface-mount electrolytic capacitors on the engine ECU (ECM) circuit board dry out, swell, and leak electrolyte over decades. The leaking acid corrodes the board traces and solder joints. This is one of the most widely documented age-related failures on the 1UZ-FE LS400 (and its SC400/Soarer siblings), and it worsens the older the car gets. Enthusiast consensus is that essentially every pre-1998 LS400/SC400 ECU is now degraded to some degree. Symptoms are erratic and intermittent, which makes it a notorious misdiagnosis trap where owners replace sensors, coils, and fuel components before finding the ECU is the root cause.
before.solution: Recap the ECU: desolder all the aged electrolytic capacitors, neutralize/clean any acid residue on the board, and install new low-ESR 105C-rated Japanese capacitors (Rubycon, Nichicon, Panasonic, Nippon Chemi-Con). 1990-92 boards use ~10-11 capacitors; 1993-94 use ~8. This is fine-pitch SMD work, not a first-time soldering job; many owners send the unit to a specialist recap/rebuild service instead.
symptoms: Random check-engine light / stored codes that don't match a bad part

before.title: Front lower ball joint wear and (rarely) separation
before.description: The front lower ball joints wear out with age and mileage and, in documented cases, have separated/sheared while driving — a serious safety concern at speed. Toyota's own maintenance schedule calls for ball-joint and suspension inspection at short intervals (about every 15,000 miles / 12 months), reflecting that these are wear items on the heavy LS400. Worn joints first show up as clunks and loose steering; total separation is the dangerous end state.
before.solution: Inspect the lower (and upper) ball joints for play at each service; replace worn joints in pairs. Use quality OEM/Aisin or reputable brands (Moog, 555) rather than the cheapest aftermarket, given the safety role. On many LS400s the ball joint is integral to the lower control arm, so a control-arm assembly may be required.
symptoms: Clunk or knock over bumps from the front
Wheel visibly loose at the joint in severe cases

before.title: Oil leaks from cam/crank seals, valve-cover gaskets, and timing cover
before.description: As the car ages, the elastomer seals and gaskets harden and weep oil. The most common sources are the valve-cover gaskets (oil drips onto the exhaust manifolds and produces a burning-oil smell), the front crankshaft and camshaft oil seals behind the timing cover, and the oil-pan gasket. On the 1998-2000 VVT-i engines, the O-ring inside the VVT-i cam phaser/gear is an additional documented leak point. Multiple sources typically leak at once on high-mileage cars.
before.solution: Replace the valve-cover gaskets (and spark-plug tube seals) for the top-end weep. For front-cover/crank/cam seal leaks, the timing belt and covers must come off — replace all three front oil seals together while access is open, ideally bundled with the timing-belt service to save labor.
symptoms: Oil drips/spots under the front of the engine
Smoke from engine bay off the exhaust manifolds

before.title: Starter motor failure buried under the intake manifold
before.description: The 1UZ-FE V8 mounts the starter in the engine valley, underneath the intake manifold, rather than at the side of the block. The starter solenoid contacts and motor wear out, typically between roughly 100,000 and 200,000 miles. The failure itself is ordinary, but the location makes it a labor-intensive job because the intake manifold must be removed to reach it. Two side complications are documented during the teardown: the plastic heater control valve commonly cracks and needs replacing, and the fragile variable-length intake runners can break if mishandled.
before.solution: Remove the intake manifold and replace the starter (a Denso reman/OEM unit is preferred for longevity). Owners are strongly advised to replace the heater control valve and any brittle vacuum/coolant hoses while the manifold is off, since access is otherwise costly to repeat. Use new intake and throttle-body gaskets on reassembly.

before.title: Timing belt / water pump service — interference risk on 1998-2000 VVT-i
before.description: The 1UZ-FE uses a rubber timing belt with a factory replacement interval of 90,000 miles or 7 years. A widely cited distinction: the 1990-1997 non-VVT-i engines are generally regarded as non-interference (a broken belt strands the car but typically does not smash valves), while the 1998-2000 VVT-i engines are commonly described as interference — a belt failure on those can cause valve-to-piston damage. On aging cars the belt itself is less often the failure point than a seized idler pulley or a failing water pump taking the belt out, so the whole kit must be serviced together.
before.solution: Replace the timing belt as a full kit at the interval: belt, both idler bearings, tensioner, and the water pump (driven by the belt). Inspect and replace the front crank and cam oil seals while the covers are off. Use OEM/Aisin or Gates components.
symptoms: Engine dies and won't restart if belt breaks
Coolant leak/overheating from failing water pump
Belt whine or rattle from a worn idler/tensioner
Coolant seepage at front of engine

before.title: Variable-assist power-steering pump/hose leaks (can kill the alternator)
before.description: The LS400 uses a variable-assist power-steering system (running ATF) whose pump seals and high-pressure hoses harden and leak with age. Because the power-steering pump sits directly above the alternator on the 1UZ-FE (worst on 1991-1997 cars), a leak drips fluid straight onto the alternator, contaminating it and causing premature charging failure. So a neglected PS leak commonly cascades into an alternator failure — the two are documented as a linked problem on these cars. Common leak points are the pump pulley/shaft seal and the high-pressure line.
before.solution: Replace the leaking power-steering pump seals and/or pressure hoses and clean up contamination promptly. If the alternator has been soaked/fouled, replace it (OEM/Denso reman). Address the leak first so a new alternator isn't ruined, and use the correct ATF (not conventional PS fluid).
symptoms: Charging warning light or dead battery from fouled alternator
Fluid dripping onto front of engine
